checks: The convex distance test places every positive source atom in the convex hull of the target atoms. Barycentric representations then give feasible rows. Prescribed row masses bound all entries, so the row polytope and its column-sum image are compact and convex.

Strict separation has the stated orientation. The lifted finite hull plus the upward ray is a polyhedron. Within the affine span of the physical hull, upward unboundedness rules out upper bounds on height and finiteness requires at least one affine lower bound. Their maximum gives the correct value even on a lower-dimensional or singleton hull and extends to a finite continuous convex test on the ambient space.

Minimizing rows independently gives the sum of source masses times the lower hull values. Convex order bounds it by the corresponding target integral, and the one-atom representations give g(y_j) at most b_j. This contradicts strict separation.

Source cube barycenters lie in the closed cubes. Target product weights are Borel, nonnegative and sum to one, with each interpolated coordinate having the original coordinate mean, including points on grid boundaries. Jensen has the claimed opposite directions for source contraction and target spreading. The exact displacement bound is the cube diameter, and a common compact box contains the grids for delta at most one.

Compactness at fixed mass and continuity of the projections give the prescribed marginals in the limit. Continuous row tests pass on the compact product. For each coordinate the finite signed displacement measure on the input box is zero by uniqueness from continuous tests, so all bounded Borel tests hold.

Disintegration for positive mass gives conditional probabilities. The Borel identities force the conditional mean by testing each coordinate on all input Borel sets. Conditional Jensen yields the reverse convex-order implication. Unequal masses preclude both sides and zero common mass gives the zero coupling.

overlap.comparison: Its proof at (6)–(9) gives the finite feasibility argument for residual laws on a common finite set. The same argument applies to the union of real atom supports with zero masses allowed, because its separation and max-affine test only use the atom vectors. Its stated recoupling theorem concerns existing arrays on finite lattice sites. The grid approximation and Borel row identity for general compactly supported marginals extend that finite argument.

Its nonnegative-convex-order criterion concerns finitely many source packets and packing into a prescribed Lebesgue volume measure, with a capacity inequality and possibly unequal masses. That specialization gives a martingale when the packets exhaust the volume, while the frozen statement allows arbitrary compact marginals of equal mass.
Its explicit simplex-law martingale compares prescribed distributions and preserves their minimum coordinate at the critical step. The arbitrary compact-marginal existence criterion has wider scope.
